entries.summary: Builders use Mastra, an open-source TypeScript framework, to create increasingly capable agents with MongoDB.
entries.text: Builders use Mastra, an open-source TypeScript framework, to create increasingly capable agents with MongoDB. But preparing retrieval for those agents can mean copying operational data into a separate collection, generating and syncing embeddings, merging semantic and keyword results, reranking, and fetching full records: a lot of code to maintain, and a lot of places for data to drift. Today, we're bringing all of it into a single query in Mastra (v1.28): Hybrid Search now works together with Automated Embedding, BYOC, pre-filtering, and Native Reranking to return the most relevant full documents from your existing collection, with no separate copy or sync job. Here's what each piece does: Hybrid Search combines semantic and keyword matching in one query, so your application doesn’t have to coordinate separate searches. Automated Embedding generates and maintains embeddings for text fields and queries, removing application-side embedding and synchronization work. Bring Your Own Collection (BYOC) lets Mastra search your existing MongoDB collection and return full documents, avoiding the need for a separate retrieval copy, ID tracking, and follow-up fetches. If you are starting a new Mastra application, we recommend using BYOC so that Mastra can query your operational data, rather than creating a separate copy for semantic search and retrieval. entries.summary: Payment platforms operate in a demanding environment. They must protect payment account data and support the teams that authorize transactions, investigate suspicious activity, and resolve exceptions.
entries.text: Payment platforms operate in a demanding environment. They must protect payment account data and support the teams that authorize transactions, investigate suspicious activity, and resolve exceptions. The more people and systems that can see sensitive data, the harder it is to control exposure. And the more data is locked away, the harder it can be to use in legitimate workflows. So how can you set up the platforms to ensure they protect that data while also giving the right people access? Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), a global security standard managed by the PCI Security Standards Council, provides a framework for protecting payment account data, restricting access, securing networks, and monitoring activity. Meeting those objectives is not a database-only exercise. It depends on how the application handles data, how the database server protects and governs it, and how the underlying infrastructure is configured and operated. While the fully managed MongoDB Atlas platform can provide a foundation for organizations pursuing PCI DSS compliance, with MongoDB’s infrastructure-level certifications supporting the infrastructure layer, some organizations opt for a self-managed architecture to maintain direct operational control over their infrastructure and internal security policies. For self-managed deployments, MongoDB Enterprise Advanced provides database security, governance, and encryption capabilities that can help support applicable PCI DSS object
entries.title: How to Align Modern Payment Platforms with PCI DSS Using MongoDB Enterprise Advanced

entries.summary: Your MongoDB Atlas metrics show elevated disk I/O, high search CPU, increasing query latency, or a rising search max replication lag.
entries.text: Your MongoDB Atlas metrics show elevated disk I/O, high search CPU, increasing query latency, or a rising search max replication lag. Like when your car’s mysterious “check engine” light comes on, these signals can mean different things. To figure out the issue, you’ll want to start by identifying which process and metric is under pressure. Scaling the database tier may provide temporary relief, but it does not separate the search and operational workloads. When mongot and mongod share nodes, search can compete with database activity for memory, disk I/O, and CPU. The right response depends on whether the index does not fit in available memory, the workloads contend during traffic spikes, or possibly even both occurring simultaneously. This post explains how to diagnose slow search performance, decide whether dedicated search nodes are the right fix, and size them correctly if they are. Why tackling the underlying issue matters The default response to slow search is often to scale up the database tier. More RAM and CPU can help the database portion of the workload, but they do not create a separate resource budget for search on a co-located deployment. Two cases can produce similar symptoms, but they call for different responses. With index-size pressure, the Search index is larger than the memory available to mongot, so queries page data from disk even when database activity is low. A larger Search tier with enough memory addresses this problem; isolation by itself does not.
entries.title: Diagnosing MongoDB Search Performance with Atlas Metrics

entries.summary: Enterprise workloads are getting bigger, more variable, and harder to predict, especially as agentic applications introduce spiky, unpredictable demand.
entries.text: Enterprise workloads are getting bigger, more variable, and harder to predict, especially as agentic applications introduce spiky, unpredictable demand. Most data platforms weren't built for this reality—to cope with demand, they bolt AI services onto aging architecture, leaving customers to manage, monitor, and pay for multiple systems to get the job done. That fragmentation slows your teams down and limits how fast and how far your agentic applications can run. In a traditional database architecture, storage is tied to the machine that runs your queries. Scaling up, adding a replica, or restoring a backup comes down to copying data from one machine to another, and the bigger the database, the longer that takes. My colleague Abhishek Chauhan calls this “storage gravity.” “Data doesn’t want to move,” he wrote for the MongoDB Engineering Blog. The bigger the data gets, the harder it pulls. MongoDB built Atlas Infinite precisely for this reality; purpose-built to absorb spikes in demand with flexible, elastic scaling. Whether you’re launching a first prototype or running at petabyte-scale in production, Atlas Infinite enables you to build on a foundation that scales with you and never forces re-architecture. With MongoDB Search and Vector Search supported on Atlas Infinite in public preview, your database and retrieval live in one platform, with nothing to stitch together. entries.summary: Today, we’re launching the MongoDB Strands Harness SDK Integration, available now as the open-source strands-mongodb Python package.
entries.text: Today, we’re launching the MongoDB Strands Harness SDK Integration, available now as the open-source strands-mongodb Python package. Strands, built and maintained by AWS, is an open-source framework for building AI agents. With this integration, MongoDB becomes the single data platform behind your Strands agents, providing: Session persistence, so agents can resume conversations and complex tasks after a restart or on a different instance. Long-term memory for facts and lessons that carry across conversations. Vector search to retrieve relevant past interactions by meaning. Strands’ MemoryManager decides what to remember and when to recall it, while MongoDB handles where it’s stored and how it’s retrieved, so there’s no custom memory code to build or maintain. And because your operational data already lives in MongoDB, agents can use Atlas Vector Search to ground their answers in it, with no copy synced to a separate vector database. What is the Strands Harness SDK? The Strands Harness SDK helps developers build AI agents. It manages the agent loop while giving developers control over how agents execute tasks and maintain context. Support for memory, sessions, and hooks lets developers shape agent behavior and connect agents to their application’s data and persistence layer. It provides pluggable storage and memory interfaces, with built-in backends for local files and Amazon S3. Integrations like this one let you swap in another backing service without rewriting your agent’s
entries.title: Persistent Sessions and Memory for Strands with MongoDB

entries.summary: When a huge surge in demand meets limited resources, an awful experience usually isn’t far behind. Fans feel it when trying to compete for concert tickets with bots and scalpers.
entries.text: When a huge surge in demand meets limited resources, an awful experience usually isn’t far behind. Fans feel it when trying to compete for concert tickets with bots and scalpers. Diners feel it when they try to get a reservation at a trendy restaurant that’s fully booked for months. Websites and applications feel it when they go viral and get an accidental DDoS from a “Reddit Hug of Death.” Unpredictable spikes in demand are only becoming more common, and scaling resources to meet them is hard. In my lifetime, I’ve seen big shifts in the amount of demand systems need to handle. First, the internet era, then the cloud era, we saw increased demand that was often predictable. Think of an annual flash sale or regular seasonality. Things might speed up, with more frequent spikes, but they were still spikes you could plan around. Then AI happened. And this is where we live now: demand that’s constant, unpredictable, and extreme, increasing in frequency and intensity at the same time. If the internet era taught customers to expect an instant response, then the AI era is teaching them to expect something else: instant value. You can snap a photo of something you want, and an agent can identify it, buy it, and have it on your doorstep tomorrow. Those capabilities cut both ways. Change now hits every layer underneath faster and harder than before. The user isn't only human anymore. Agents are in the product too. Agents don’t ease in. The second they’re on, they hit your system with mas
entries.title: AI Demand is Constant, Unpredictable, and Extreme. MongoDB is Built for It.

entries.summary: At 8 a.m., a $4 million payroll is due, but an expected customer payment hasn’t arrived. Leafy International’s treasury agent spots the gap in live payment data.
entries.text: At 8 a.m., a $4 million payroll is due, but an expected customer payment hasn’t arrived. Leafy International’s treasury agent spots the gap in live payment data. It checks current balances and recommends a cash sweep from an overnight deposit. It’s enough to fund payroll while keeping Leafy’s $1 million minimum cash buffer intact. Just as the treasurer reviews the proposal, an approved, time-stamped market feed flags a material EUR/USD move after a central bank announcement. The agent connects the signal to Leafy’s upcoming euro payment, refreshes the exposure, and flags it for review. A market alert is a reason to reassess, not permission to trade. The treasurer views the rationale, data source, and update time, and then approves or delegates within the agreed mandate. If a balance, payment status, or foreign exchange (FX) rate changes before execution, the agent checks again. This is agentic treasury: Monitoring relevant conditions, recommending next steps, and helping carry them out only when authorized. Leafy International is fictional, but the pressures and actions are real. Treasury teams are exploring how AI can improve decisions across payments, cash, working capital, and financial risk—and how to govern these systems. Agentic treasury has two key requirements: Context that stays current as balances, payments, and markets move An independent check that confirms each action is authorized before it runs. MongoDB provides the data layer for both, keeping the agent's cont
entries.title: Agentic Treasury: How AI Agents Turn Cash Blind Spots Into Real-Time, Governed Action

entries.summary: Real-time analytics on live operational data, built so applications and AI agents can act on what’s happening now. The most valuable analytics no longer live in a dashboard.
entries.text: Real-time analytics on live operational data, built so applications and AI agents can act on what’s happening now. The most valuable analytics no longer live in a dashboard. They live inside the application. A logistics app reroutes a shipment around a delay. A retail system reorders inventory before the shelf goes empty. A payments platform flags unusual behavior before the transaction clears. Each of these decisions requires comparing live operational data against historical patterns. Which routes are backing up, and is that normal? What’s selling faster than usual, and should we restock? Is this login typical for this account at this time of day? Enterprises that can answer these questions in the moment adapt as conditions change. Those that can’t are reacting to yesterday. Data infrastructure has long been split into two worlds: operational databases that run applications, and data warehouses that analyze what already happened. That paradigm was built for humans looking at morning dashboards, where data a few hours or days old was fine. As analytics moved into applications, real-time analytics emerged as a category of its own, combining complex queries over massive datasets with the speed, freshness, and concurrency that live applications demand. Agents raise the bar on all three. They act continuously, can drive thousands of concurrent queries, and need sub-second answers on fresh data. As businesses rely more on agents, real-time analytics becomes a core part of their d
entries.title: MongoDB Acquires Firebolt to Bring Lightning-Fast Real-Time Analytics Into Its Intelligent Data Platform

entries.summary: Ask an underwriter to describe a policy, and you’ll get a coherent answer: A contract, for a customer, covering a car or a house, with a handful of coverages, each with a limit and a deductible, plus a history of every…
entries.text: Ask an underwriter to describe a policy, and you’ll get a coherent answer: A contract, for a customer, covering a car or a house, with a handful of coverages, each with a limit and a deductible, plus a history of every change since it was issued. One policy—with parts. Many parts. Now ask your database the same question. In most insurance core systems, that single policy is sliced across dozens of relational tables: one each for coverages, vehicles, named parties, endorsements, and billing schedules. Every time a screen loads, the system reassembles the policy by joining those tables back together. Every time a product changes, several of the tables need altering. When Manulife(1) rebuilt its policy servicing platform, its chief architect described replacing more than 500 core tables with one document per policy and reported that the new system won overwhelming approval from its developers. That gap—between how the business thinks about a policy and how the database stores it—is the central problem a document database like MongoDB solves. This blog post explains the one design decision that matters most when you make that move and why it’s an insurance decision as much as a technical one. One rule drives everything A document database stores records as nested structures, closer to a folder than a spreadsheet row. A policy document can hold its coverages, its vehicles, its parties, and its event history all within itself. The temptation is to simply pour the old table diagram
entries.title: How to Model an Insurance Policy Without Joining Dozens of Tables

entries.summary: Sometimes the biggest performance gains come not from making core operations faster, but from eliminating unnecessary work surrounding them.
entries.text: Sometimes the biggest performance gains come not from making core operations faster, but from eliminating unnecessary work surrounding them. That is exactly what we discovered while optimizing document lookup in MongoDB Atlas Search and Vector Search. By removing redundant query planning and execution overhead, we made search queries up to 5x faster without changing the underlying search algorithms. When you run a $search or $vectorSearch query in MongoDB, two key stages work together to deliver the results. First, mongot, MongoDB's search process powered by Apache Lucene, executes the search query to identify and rank the most relevant documents. Then, mongod joins the search results with the corresponding BSON documents from the underlying collection using their _ids. The resulting documents can be further processed by additional aggregation pipeline stages before being returned to the application. Figure 1 illustrates this two-stage process: Figure 1. Search execution in mongot and document materialization in mongod. This second stage, known as document materialization, is handled by an internal aggregation stage called $_internalSearchIdLookup. While search execution has been extensively optimized, we discovered that document lookup had become a significant performance bottleneck. For every matching document, the stage repeatedly constructed a new query plan and acquired collection resources, introducing substantial overhead for queries returning hundreds or thousands of
entries.title: Optimizing Document Lookup: Making Atlas Search and Vector Search Up to 5x Faster

entries.summary: Retail is entering the era of the multi-agent shopping assistant.
entries.text: Retail is entering the era of the multi-agent shopping assistant. Instead of a single, stateless chatbot following a rigid script, retailers are building systems where multiple agents collaborate behind the scenes, drawing on preferences and customer purchase history to deliver recommendations that improve with every interaction. More retailers are reconfiguring their backends to reflect the rise in agentic usage, as this is no small trend: McKinsey estimates AI agents could mediate $3 trillion to $5 trillion of global consumer commerce by 2030.(1) The need is real, as the race is heating up to quickly respond to customer searches and take service to another level. A customer searching for a pair of running shoes for an upcoming marathon no longer triggers a keyword search. The query kicks off a coordinated reasoning process across multiple specialized agents. This has to happen rapidly and seamlessly to keep consumers' attention and needs met. The promise of this shift is real, but the real architectural question has nothing to do with which LLM or orchestration framework a team chooses. It has everything to do with where the data lives and whether every agent can see the same version of the truth simultaneously. Increasingly, retailers are finding that solution in MongoDB. The technology challenge behind multi-agent AI Building a single AI agent is straightforward with modern LLMs and orchestration frameworks. Building a production multi-agent system is not. Why? entries.title: The $5 Trillion Shift: Preparing Retail Backends for the Age of AI Agents

MongoDB's flexible document model enables rapid iteration as AI models evolve, while its scalability—supporting over 100 clusters and 50+ TB of data—has made it the trusted system of record powering our platform's intelligence layer. Recently, the team wanted to continue scaling with MongoDB in a way that preserved application availability, reduced operational risk, and created a predictable runway for continued data growth. The team partnered with MongoDB Consulting’s professional services to scale a production-critical MongoDB Atlas deployment to support Observe.AI’s conversation intell

entries.summary: We are excited to announce the release of the MongoDB Vercel AI SDK integration, which provides AI applications and agents built with Vercel’s SDK with a persistent memory store in MongoDB Atlas.
entries.text: We are excited to announce the release of the MongoDB Vercel AI SDK integration, which provides AI applications and agents built with Vercel’s SDK with a persistent memory store in MongoDB Atlas. It's now open source and generally available on npm. This integration adds MongoDB Atlas as the memory store in the existing Vercel AI SDK code. Once installed, the package connects Vercel AI SDK applications to MongoDB Atlas and automatically stores the application's memories in documents. This allows the application to retain memories about conversations, user facts, and past events that persist across sessions, users, and restarts. What is the Vercel AI SDK? The Vercel AI SDK is a TypeScript toolkit for building AI applications. It handles calling models, streaming responses, using tools, and running agents that work through multi-step tasks. The SDK doesn't include a database to persist memories between runs. Without memory, an AI application starts every conversation with no knowledge of the last one. It doesn't know who the user is, what they asked yesterday, or what it learned along the way. It doesn’t have any context. Today, developers have to build their own tooling to store memories in a layer. That usually means designing a database schema, writing jobs to clear out old data, and setting up vector search so the application can find relevant past information by semantic meaning instead of just keywords. It's a lot of work to build an AI application that can remember contex
entries.title: Introducing the MongoDB Vercel AI SDK Integration: Persistent Memory for AI Applications

entries.summary: The Claude Agent SDK is a package that lets you embed Claude Code's own agent loop directly into your application: web search, file search, file editing, MCP server connections, and more, all without having to define…
entries.text: The Claude Agent SDK is a package that lets you embed Claude Code's own agent loop directly into your application: web search, file search, file editing, MCP server connections, and more, all without having to define those tools or manage the agent loop yourself. The SDK also automatically persists session transcripts to the local file system by default. Claude calls it the Agent SessionStore. Today, we are excited to announce the MongoDB Claude SDK Session Adapter, available in Python (with TypeScript coming in January 2027). What is the Claude Agent SessionStore? But first, let's understand what a SessionStore actually is. It is the extension point in the Claude Agent SDK for saving an agent's session outside the machine where it ran. Configure one, and the SDK mirrors every conversation turn and action as the agent works, so the session can pick back up exactly where it left off, on any instance that has access to that store. That matters most once an agent stops running on a single, persistent machine. Say a team deploys their Claude agent as a Lambda function, callable as an internal service by teams across the company. Every invocation is a disposable instance; there's no local disk to store anything between calls. Without a SessionStore, each request is stateless by default; the agent has no memory of what came before. With a configured SessionStore, any invocation can pick up a session's full history, regardless of which instance handled the last turn. That is the gap
entries.title: Introducing the MongoDB Claude SDK Session Adapter: Durable Session Storage for Agents

entries.summary: We’re excited to announce the MongoDB Google ADK Integration, which provides developers with the building blocks they need to create durable memory for agent state.
entries.text: We’re excited to announce the MongoDB Google ADK Integration, which provides developers with the building blocks they need to create durable memory for agent state. As agents move from prototypes to real-world applications, they need secure, dependable access to data and the ability to retain context over a long time. However, developers still need to build their own tooling for a data store that provides durable agent memory for agent state. This integration gives developers a cohesive, ADK-native experience for using MongoDB as the data platform for agents. What is the Google ADK? The Google Agent Development Kit (ADK) is an open source agent development framework that lets you build, debug, and deploy reliable AI agents at enterprise scale. It is available in Python, TypeScript, Go, Java, and Kotlin. Google ADK offers developers an extensive set of tools for creating, deploying, assessing, and scaling agents, enabling developers to build anything from personal AI assistants to mission-critical business workflows. How does the MongoDB Google ADK Integration help? Developers can prototype an agent that searches a product catalog or knowledge base, then evolve it into a production experience that preserves user context across conversations and recalls relevant prior interactions. entries.title: Introducing the MongoDB Google ADK Integration: Durable Memory for Agent State

entries.summary: Exciting developments are on the horizon for users of Microsoft Azure, marking a significant leap in data management capabilities.
entries.text: Exciting developments are on the horizon for users of Microsoft Azure, marking a significant leap in data management capabilities. First off, Atlas Data Federation is now Generally Available on Azure. Atlas Data Federation is now generally available for deployment in Azure. An Azure deployment can query data in Microsoft Azure Blob Storage, alongside other supported sources. And that's not all. We've also launched the General Availability of Atlas Online Archive on Azure. These advancements usher in a new era of efficient archiving solutions for Azure-based data solutions. Both updates are big steps forward in making data management on Azure more powerful and flexible. Let's dive into what this means for you! Azure support in Atlas Data Federation (General Availability) Atlas Data Federation can query across multiple supported sources, including Atlas clusters and cloud object storage. entries.text: Automated Embedding is now available in Public Preview on MongoDB Atlas. When we introduced Automated Embedding to MongoDB Vector Search in MongoDB Community Edition, we started from a single principle: developers building agentic applications shouldn't have to operate a parallel embedding pipeline just to search their own data. That release proved the pattern: text in, text out, no client-side embedding code. On MongoDB Atlas, it goes further, using Voyage AI embedding models to solve the operational problems that have made vector search the most fragile part of an agent stack. Figure 1. Automated Embedding flow in MongoDB Atlas. Your vector search index falls behind your data A document gets edited. The vector store still has the old embedding. The agent retrieves stale context and confidently answers based on outdated information. The fix has historically been a backfill job, written by a human, scheduled by a human, and debugged by a human. The time between "data changed" and "index reflects it" is measured in hours, not seconds. Automated Embedding solves this with field-level delta detection. When a document changes, MongoDB Atlas re-embeds only when an indexed field actually changes. Sync is near real-time, not batch. There is no manual re-index path because there's no manual index to maintain. For agents, this is the difference between trustworthy memory and stale context. The same property extends to search on views. If your embedding source is a $concat of title, ca

entries.summary: Almost nothing is as important to someone today as their financial health.
entries.text: Almost nothing is as important to someone today as their financial health. Most of us want to stay on top of what's happening with our bank accounts, like when a deposit clears so we can pay bills, if we're reaching our credit card limit, or if we have finally paid off that 30-year mortgage and can free up funds for that dream vacation or paying for our kid's college tuition. But we don't always get immediate feedback when transactions happen. That information often sits on the backend within our banks, and then days or weeks later we may get an email or alert with advice on investing or creating a payment plan. But with actionable banking, this all becomes immediate. With the help of agentic AI, banks’ customers can quickly have a better understanding of steps they can take to make an investment or curb their spending with AI-powered insights. And people have said they want this. In fact, in a survey conducted by Personetics of 2,000 bank customers(1), 70% said they strongly want their bank to proactively analyze their financial situation and 84% said they would likely switch to a bank that offers timely, relevant advice. Actionable banking is also the safest first step toward autonomous banking. The agents act on events, but a human still makes the decision. MongoDB Atlas makes this possible by turning banking events into real-time triggers, unifying customer context in one platform, and keeping an auditable record of every agent action. entries.text: As enterprise AI agent adoption scales, the absence of centralized, organization-level tool infrastructure is producing compounding costs. When adoption is built around optimizing for deployment speed, enterprises expose themselves to a combination of risks: duplicated engineering effort, security exposure, and operational opacity. Every enterprise needs its own shared tool registry, one that reflects its specific regulatory environment, security posture, and operational conventions. To be clear, this is not an argument for a public package manager, something like npm, PyPI, or Maven. The infrastructure each enterprise needs is internal; scoped to its own teams, its own data, its own policies, its own domain. Trying to expand the scope beyond the confines of individual organizations would be premature standardization in a fast-moving, nascent space. A shared enterprise tool registry is not an optimization or a nice-to-have. It is foundational infrastructure as agent deployments scale beyond early experiments. The case for it rests on two pillars: reducing coordination cost and enabling risk management, both for the humans building with agents and for the agents themselves. AI agents depend on tools that retrieve data, write records, trigger workflows, and call external APIs. According to McKinsey, in most large organizations, these tools are built by individual teams in an ad hoc fashion: undocumented, ungoverned, and invisible to the rest of the organization. This pattern is

entries.text: Editor’s note: This post is the second in a five-part series exploring how MongoDB Atlas Resource Policies help you strengthen database security and enforce consistent guardrails across your organization. Read the first post on IP access list management here. Future posts will cover topics like blocking wildcard IP access and restricting access by cloud provider or region. Imagine protecting your home with only a front-door lock. No matter how good that lock is, what happens when someone breaks a window or tricks their way in? A single security control, no matter how robust, creates a single point of failure. Database security faces the same reality. Defense-in-depth is a military strategy adapted for cybersecurity: Deploy multiple independent layers of security controls so that if one fails, others still provide protection. In database security, this means protecting multiple dimensions simultaneously. Network controls determine who can reach your database, geographic controls ensure data stays in compliant regions, and protocol controls protect data in transit. Each layer requires different knowledge and tools to bypass, making comprehensive attacks substantially more difficult. MongoDB Atlas Resource Policies enable defense-in-depth at the infrastructure layer, preventing misconfigurations before deployments happen rather than detecting problems after resources go live. Each policy addresses a different attack vector: network access, geographic restrictions, and protocol r
entries.title: Layer MongoDB Atlas Resource Policies for Defense-in-Depth

Picture this: Your development team spins up a new MongoDB cluster for a critical application. To get things working quickly, the team adds overly permissive IP access rules. That might mean allowing their entire office network’s /16 CIDR block, or perhaps skipping careful validation of which specific IPs truly need access. That cluster goes into production. Six months later, during a security audit, you discover your database has been accessible from far more locations than anyone realized, with no clear documentation of who added which IP addresses or why. Scenarios like this aren’t uncommon—and highlight why customers rely on MongoDB Atlas’ IP Access Lists to enforce clear, least-privilege network boundaries. IP Access Lists are a critical defensive layer in a defense-in-depth approach to security. What if you could define exactly which IP addresses are allowed to access your databases and make it technically impossible for anyone to deviate from that approved list, at scale? These models are suitable for CPU-only deployments (no GPU), as well as IoT and mobile devices, with no internet connection required. Note: We are publishing these models and the recipe used to train them as a contribution to the open source community. They have been developed by the ML team of MongoDB Research. The models are published under a permissive Apache 2.0 license and offered as is, without any explicit or implied support. At the time of writing, they are not used in any of MongoDB's commercial products or service offerings. The challenges Modern text embedding models have delivered huge gains in natural language processing tasks, from question‑answering to RAGs. But these gains come at a cost: Model sizes are exploding. entries.summary: Where money moves, crime evolves.
entries.text: Where money moves, crime evolves. As banking becomes fully digital—with instant payments, open finance APIs, and mobile-first onboarding—it has opened new roads for cyberattacks, forcing financial institutions to respond in real-time. With just seconds to detect, prevent, and react to suspicious activity—without disrupting the customer experience—banks face an immense challenge that only modern, AI-powered solutions can meet. Welcome to our new series on mitigating financial crime with MongoDB. In the Financial Crime Mitigation series (this is the first of five posts we have planned!), you will learn how to build modern, anti-fincrime platforms that keep pace with increasingly automated, AI-assisted adversaries. Let’s begin by understanding what financial crime is and why it matters. A trillion-dollar problem Financial crime encompasses illicit activities that exploit the financial system, from sophisticated money laundering schemes to AI-powered synthetic identity fraud. The numbers are staggering. According to the Global Financial and Economic Crime Outlook, global financial institutions' losses could reach over $2 trillion USD due to financial crime each year. Putting this in perspective, these losses may represent 3.5% of global GDP, with an expectation of having this figure nearly double to $6 trillion by 2030. But financial crime doesn’t just cause monetary losses. It also undermines customer trust, harms brand reputation, disrupts operations, and diminishes conversion

entries.text: Every customer relationship is an investment, and like any investment, its value grows over time—when relationships are properly nurtured. Industry research has shown that retaining existing customers is far more cost-effective than acquiring new ones. For example, a 2025 article by Startup Guru Lab states that “businesses spend 5 to 7 times more to acquire new customers compared to keeping existing ones.” New customers require significant marketing spend, extensive onboarding efforts, and a sustained period of trust-building before they can reach the level of loyalty and profitability of an existing customer. In contrast, customers who have already purchased from a brand have overcome those initial barriers. They know the products, the service standards, and the overall brand promise. What’s more, return customers tend to purchase more frequently, spend more per transaction, and are far more likely to recommend the brand to others. Despite this well-documented return on investment, many retailers still focus the majority of their resources on acquisition rather than retention. A 2024 report by The CMO Survey notes how marketers spend “19.6% more on acquiring customers than retaining them.” Marketing campaigns often prioritize bringing in fresh traffic over protecting the relationships that already exist. The simple truth is that preventing a customer from leaving is almost always faster, cheaper, and more impactful than replacing them. When retailers proactively address sign

entries.text: Transaction routing is a delicate balancing act between authorization rates, execution cost, and latency. A declined transaction can mean a lost sale, making payment optimization one of the most direct levers for top-line revenue growth. Yet payment operations teams remain trapped in manual operational cycles: Pulling batch CSV reports, analyzing spreadsheets, and manually updating rule tables in legacy gateways. And that repetitive cycle can cost you dearly. Global businesses lose 1.5% to 2.2% of annual revenue to poor payment performance and false declines, according to research by Checkout.com and Oxford Economics. While those percentages may seem small, it actually adds up to more than $50 billion in lost revenue each year. And the impact isn’t seen in weeks, months, or a year later. In fact, the fallout is immediate: 45% of shoppers abandon purchases and shift to competitors after a single checkout decline. To recover lost revenue, modern infrastructure must decouple routing intelligence from checkout execution. Running a background multi-agent control plane to analyze telemetry, simulate options, enforce cost guardrails, and update JSON rules in MongoDB enables continuous smart routing optimization with execution in milliseconds. Welcome to our new series on agentic payment smart routing, where we architect a modern payment routing platform. entries.text: This guest post by independent security researcher Ben Zimmermann was developed in collaboration with the Kingfisher team at MongoDB. Ben specializes in large-scale credential exposure research across public source-hosting platforms. TL;DR: I scanned 7,256,531 public repositories on Gitee (China's largest indigenous Git hosting platform), using both TruffleHog and Kingfisher, and found 26,400 unique verified-live credentials. Findings included an active organization-admin credential for a major enterprise AI platform and thousands of live cloud provider access keys. What is Gitee? Gitee, launched in 2013 by OSChina, was selected by China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology as the country's national open-source code hosting platform. Its public API is severely constrained relative to GitHub and GitLab: no paginated projects endpoint, and the on-site code-search feature appears to have been retired years ago. A 2021 attempt to study credential exposure on Gitee concluded that its APIs were too limited to scale the research. Like any large Git platform, it's an attractive surface for credential exposure: It is Git-based, so secrets buried deep in commit history persist. It hosts millions of public repositories with active commit volume. It has no public equivalent of the platform-vendor secret-scanning partnerships that have become standard on GitHub. entries.summary: JetBrains released a new version of DataGrip that includes support for MongoDB and ships with the MongoDB Shell out of the box.
entries.text: JetBrains released a new version of DataGrip that includes support for MongoDB and ships with the MongoDB Shell out of the box. A few months ago, JetBrains released the first version of DataGrip that supports MongoDB. DataGrip is a professional DataBase IDE and is a great tool for advanced data exploration and analytical queries for your data in MongoDB and Atlas. If you use any of the other JetBrains commercial products for development (e.g. PhpStorm, PyCharm), you can install the Database Tools plugin and work with MongoDB right inside your IDE. As we announced last week at MongoDB.live, the MongoDB plugin in DataGrip and in the other JetBrains IDE now includes a database console built on top of the MongoDB Shell. This is the result of a close collaboration between engineering teams at MongoDB and JetBrains and we are excited to finally release it to all our users. With this integration, when you connect to MongoDB and Atlas with DataGrip, you get a console/shell experience that is 100% consistent with what you get in the terminal or in the other MongoDB’s developer tools. DataGrip and Atlas When your data is stored in Atlas, navigating through it with DataGrip is extremely easy. For example, to connect to my free Atlas cluster, I can just grab a connection string from the Atlas UI, use it to add a new data source in DataGrip and I am connected and ready to explore my data. entries.summary: The question of what the term “sovereign cloud” means in Europe has moved from policy debates to formal European Commission (EC) procurement frameworks and industrial investments.
entries.text: The question of what the term “sovereign cloud” means in Europe has moved from policy debates to formal European Commission (EC) procurement frameworks and industrial investments. The Cloud Sovereignty Framework (CSF), Sovereignty Effectiveness Assurance Levels (SEAL), and the developing EU Cybersecurity Certification Scheme for Cloud Services (EUCS) are separate initiatives that provide distinct reference points. Alongside strategic capital mobilization under the Strategic Technologies for Europe Platform (STEP), they establish a clearer direction for critical cloud infrastructure. While specific to EU institutional tenders and funding programs rather than acting as universal mandates, this combined momentum offers IT leaders and enterprise architects across regulated sectors a concrete reference point for how sovereignty criteria shape long-term architectural thinking. These developments help illustrate that operating in a regulated market does not mean every workload must remain on-premises; instead, they demonstrate that sovereignty is a spectrum, helping organizations evaluate the specific level of data control their architecture truly requires. As organizations evaluate these models, the critical question is not just which infrastructure provider can meet tech sovereignty expectations, but whether the rest of the technology stack upholds that sovereignty posture once workloads are deployed. entries.title: How MongoDB Fits into the EU Sovereign Cloud Ecosystem

entries.summary: Many of the agent demos published this year are some version of the same thing: connect your agent to a data source, let it get familiar with the data, and get a report back.
entries.text: Many of the agent demos published this year are some version of the same thing: connect your agent to a data source, let it get familiar with the data, and get a report back. We’ll build a coordinator agent and three sub-agents that search a roughly 2,900-page federal rulemaking docket, write their findings to a shared workspace, and hand off to a fourth agent that reconciles the findings into a memo. You'll interrupt the pipeline mid-run, restart it, and confirm it resumes from the last completed stage instead of redoing finished work. Working through it cost us $2 to $5 in API calls and took about 45 minutes. Specifically, you will: Load a mixed-format document corpus into Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3) and index it in MongoDB Atlas. Watch an agent navigate that corpus incrementally instead of loading it into a prompt. Build a coordinator that delegates to three sub-agents sharing one workspace. Interrupt a running pipeline and resume it from saved run state, without redoing completed work. This tutorial moves from architecture (what's searched vs. what's stored in bytes), to a single-agent search example, to a four-agent pipeline, to failure recovery, to production caveats. The complete code and corpus are in the companion repository (GenAI-Showcase, partners/langchain/langchain-deepagents). What is a virtual filesystem? A virtual filesystem is a path-based interface that abstracts away where file bytes actually live. An agent sees a path such as corpus/rules/88FR21752
entries.title: Give Deep Agents a Searchable Filesystem on MongoDB Atlas

entries.summary: I spent a large part of my career working in banking and logistics.
entries.text: I spent a large part of my career working in banking and logistics. In logistics, I spent more than eight years working across different stages of logistics systems, from development to implementation and production support. That experience shaped the way I think about technology. Knowing a tool or framework is important, but what interests me most is understanding the business problem behind it and where technology can actually add value. A few weeks ago, I returned as a speaker to a company where I had worked for many years. Being back there reminded me of several day-to-day logistical challenges and made me wonder how I would approach those problems today. That is where the Agentic Warehouse Management System came from. With this project, I am not trying to build a complete WMS. Instead, I want to use a logistics scenario I know well to explore how an AI agent can become part of a real business workflow and where it can add value. In this first part, we will introduce the WMS scenario and identify where an AI agent can help. In Part 2, we will define and connect the agent using Java and Spring AI. Finally, in Part 3, we will execute the plan, gather context, make the replenishment decision, and act when necessary.
